facts.statement: Cedarpelta lived in Utah during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically between 98.2 and 93 million years ago.
facts.quote: Cedarpelta is an extinct genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from Utah that lived during the Late Cretaceous period (Cenomanian to lower Turonian stage, 98.2 to 93 Ma)

facts.statement: The genus Cedarpelta was named in 2001 by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Don Burge, and John Bird.
facts.quote: It was named in 2001 by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Don Burge, and John Bird.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cedarpelta were discovered by Evan Hall and Sue Ann Bilbey near the Price River in Carbon County, Utah.
facts.quote: The partial remains of an ankylosaur were discovered by Evan Hall and Sue Ann Bilbey at the CEM site near the Price River in Carbon County, Utah

facts.statement: The species name bilbeyhallorum honors the discoverers Sue Ann Bilbey and Evan Hall.
facts.quote: The specific name, bilbeyhallorum, honours Sue Ann Bilbey and Evan Hall, who discovered the remains of Cedarpelta.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta is estimated to have been 7 meters long and weighed 5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Cedarpelta has an estimated length of 7 metres (23 feet) and weight of 5 tonnes (11,023 lbs).

facts.statement: Cedarpelta is one of the few known ankylosaurs whose individual skull bones were not completely fused together.
facts.quote: The skull of Cedarpelta lacks extensive cranial ornamentation and is one of the only known ankylosaurs with individual skull bones that are not completely fused together.

facts.statement: Two skulls of Cedarpelta are known, with an estimated length of roughly 60 centimeters.
facts.quote: Two skulls are known, and the skull length for Cedarpelta is estimated to have been roughly 60 cm.

facts.statement: One Cedarpelta skull was found disarticulated, providing the first opportunity to examine individual ankylosaur skull bones rather than a fused unit.
facts.quote: One of the Cedarpelta skulls was found disarticulated, a first for an ankylosaur skull, allowing paleontologists a unique opportunity to examine the individual bones instead of being limited to an ossified unit.

facts.statement: Adult Cedarpelta skulls lack a distinctive pattern of fused head tiles (caputegulae).
facts.quote: The skulls, though of large and thus not juvenile individuals, do not show a distinctive pattern of fused caputegulae, head tiles.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta possesses premaxillary teeth, a trait inherited from earlier Ornithischians.
facts.quote: The presence of premaxillary teeth is a plesiomorphic character because it is inherited from earlier Ornithischia.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta exhibits the closure of the lateral temporal fenestra, an advanced trait found only in ankylosaurids.
facts.quote: In contrast, closure of the opening on the side of the skull behind the orbit, the lateral temporal fenestra, is an advanced, derived (apomorphic) character only known in ankylosaurid ankylosaurians.

facts.statement: Carpenter (2001) classified Cedarpelta within the family Ankylosauridae.
facts.quote: Carpenter (2001) placed Cedarpelta within the family Ankylosauridae and offered two interpretations of its position.

facts.statement: Researchers have debated whether Cedarpelta represents the most basal known ankylosaurid.
facts.quote: The first was that it could be the basalmost known ankylosaurid, i.e. the first discovered branch to split off from the ankylosaurid stem line.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Cedarpelta formed an early ankylosaurid clade called Shamosaurinae alongside Gobisaurus and Shamosaurus.
facts.quote: The second was that it formed an early ankylosaurid branch, or clade, Shamosaurinae together with Gobisaurus of north-central China and the eponymous Shamosaurus of Mongolia.

facts.statement: Vickaryous et al. (2004) interpreted Cedarpelta as the most basal member of the family Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: Vickaryous et al. (2004) interpreted Cedarpelta as the basalmost member of the family Nodosauridae, positioned even below the nodosaurids Pawpawsaurus, Silvisaurus, and Sauropelta.

facts.statement: Carpenter proposed that in Cedarpelta, skull armor ossified in an intermediate layer called the periosteum, rather than directly from skin or skull bones.
facts.quote: The lack of a clear pattern in Cedarpelta suggested to Carpenter that the ossification took place in an intermediate layer between the scales and the skull roof itself, which he surmised to have been the periosteum.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta lived in North America during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 110 to 100 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 110 y 100 millones de años, entre el Albiense y Aptiense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta was a large ankylosaur.
facts.quote: Cedarpelta era un gran anquilosaurio.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the body length at 7 meters and the weight at 5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul indicó una longitud corporal de 7 metros y un peso de 5 toneladas.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter calculated the length to be smaller than 5 meters.
facts.quote: Kenneth Carpenter lo calculó más pequeño de 5 metros.

facts.statement: Each premaxilla possessed six conical teeth.
facts.quote: Cada premaxilar tiene seis dientes cónicos.

facts.statement: Two skulls are known, with an estimated cranial length of approximately 60 centimeters.
facts.quote: Se conocen dos cráneos, y se estima que la longitud del cráneo para Cedarpelta fue de aproximadamente 60 centímetros.

facts.statement: The maxilla contained eighteen teeth.
facts.quote: El maxilar tiene dieciocho dientes.

facts.statement: Sue Ann Bilbey and Evan Hall discovered a quarry with ankylosaur remains near the Price River in Carbon County, Utah, in 1990.
facts.quote: En 1990, Sue Ann Bilbey y Evan Hall descubrieron una cantera con restos de anquilosáuridos cerca del río Price en el condado de Carbon, Utah.

facts.statement: The type species Cedarpelta bilbeyhallorum was named and described by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge, and John Bird in 2001.
facts.quote: En 2001, la especie tipo Cedarpelta bilbeyhallorum fue nombrada y descrita por Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge y John Bird.

facts.statement: The generic name means "cedar mountain shield," referencing the Cedar Mountain Formation and the animal's armored plates, while the specific name honors the discoverers of the holotype.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico significa "escudo de la montaña del cedro", llamada así por la Formación Cedar Mountain y las placas acorazadas del animal, del griego pelte, "escudo pequeño" y el nombre específico que honra a Sue Ann Bilbey y Evan Hall como los descubridores del holotipo.

facts.statement: The fossils are now assigned to the base of the Mussentuchit Member, dating between 116 and 109 million years ago at the Aptian-Albian boundary.
facts.quote: Originalmente se pensó que estos sitios pertenecían al miembro Ruby Ranch de la formación Montaña Cedar, pero ahora están asignados a la base del miembro Mussentuchit que lo cubre, que tiene entre 116 y 109 millones de años, aproximadamente en el límite Aptiense - Albiense.

facts.statement: Carpenter and colleagues placed the taxon within the family Ankylosauridae.
facts.quote: Carpenter y colegas colocaron el taxón dentro de la familia Ankylosauridae.

facts.statement: Vickaryous et al. in 2004 interpreted the genus as the most basal member of the family Nodosauridae, placed below Pawpawsaurus, Silvisaurus, and Sauropelta.
facts.quote: Vickaryous et al. en 2004, sin embargo, interpretaron el género como el miembro más basal de la familia Nodosauridae, colocado incluso debajo de los nodosáuridos Pawpawsaurus campbelli, Silvisaurus condrayi y Sauropelta edwardsorum.

facts.statement: However, new skeletal material confirmed Carpenter's original identification that Cedarpelta is one of the most basal ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, el nuevo material del esqueleto confirma la identificación original de Carpenter y colegas de Cedarpelta es uno de los anquilosáuridos más basales.

facts.statement: One Cedarpelta skull was found disarticulated, the first for an ankylosaurid skull, allowing paleontologists to examine individual bones rather than an ossified unit.
facts.quote: Uno de los cráneos de Cedarpelta se encontró desarticulado, el primero para un cráneo de anquilosáurido, lo que permite a los paleontólogos una oportunidad única para examinar los huesos individuales en lugar de limitarse a una unidad osificada.

facts.statement: The lack of a clear pattern in Cedarpelta suggested to Carpenter that ossification occurred in an intermediate layer between the scales and the skull roof, which he hypothesized was the periosteum.
facts.quote: La falta de un patrón claro en Cedarpelta le sugirió a Carpenter que la osificación tuvo lugar en una capa intermedia entre las escamas y el techo del cráneo en sí, que supuso que era el periostio.

facts.statement: No tail club or mace is known for Cedarpelta, but researchers emphasized that early ankylosaurs might have lacked a true tail club.
facts.quote: No se conoce ninguna porra o maza de cola de Cedarpelta, pero Arbor enfatizó que los primeros anquilosáurido podrían haber carecido de una porra verdadera.

facts.statement: Cedarpelta lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)
